articles.title: Rochdale's Year as Town of Culture Generates Over £5.5 Million for Local Economy
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's designation as Greater Manchester's Town of Culture has resulted in more than £5.5 million in economic benefits, with over 213,000 attendees at nearly 300 events throughout the year.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's year as Greater Manchester's Town of Culture has proven to be a significant economic boon, generating over £5.5 million for the local economy, according to a recent report from Rochdale Council. The evaluation highlighted that the borough attracted 213,099 attendees across 297 events during the 2025/2026 year, showcasing the impact of cultural initiatives on community engagement and local spending.

The council's assessment, based on a conservative estimate of £25 spent per attendee, indicates that the actual economic impact could be as high as £16.6 million, considering a higher daily visitor spend of £78 suggested by Marketing Manchester. This financial boost follows the council's successful application for £50,000 from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) Culture Fund to support cultural activities from April 2025 to March 2026.

Major events that contributed to this success included 'The Herds', Street Eat, the Rochdale Comedy Festival, Rochdale Pride, and the Ignite Fire Festival. These events not only attracted visitors but also provided paid opportunities for local artists and freelancers, enhancing the cultural landscape of the borough. The report also noted a significant increase in engagement from younger audiences and diverse communities, with 94 percent of attendees feeling that the events positively enhanced Rochdale's image.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation, expressed pride in the achievements of the year, stating that the momentum created would serve as a strong foundation for future cultural investments and events. The council plans to continue hosting large-scale events to build on the legacy of the Town of Culture status, ensuring ongoing benefits for the local community.

articles.title: Prime Minister Calls for Accountability in Michael Hoolickin Murder Case
articles.excerpt: The family of Michael Hoolickin, murdered in Middleton in 2016, has welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for accountability regarding failures in the probation system that contributed to his death.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

03:09, 04 September 2026

The family of Michael Hoolickin, murdered in Middleton in 2016, has expressed support for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for accountability regarding failures in the probation system that contributed to his death.

02:50, 04 September 2026

The family of Michael Hoolickin, murdered in Middleton in 2016, has welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's call for accountability regarding failures in the probation system that contributed to his death.

The family of Michael Hoolickin, a 27-year-old father murdered in Middleton in 2016, has expressed support for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent call for accountability concerning the probation system's failures that contributed to his death. Michael was killed by an offender who had a history of violent crime and had been under probation supervision despite numerous breaches of his licence.

Michael Hoolickin was stabbed outside the Friendship Inn on Cheapside on October 14, 2016, by an individual who had previously been jailed for violent offences, including biting off a man's ear. Despite over 50 breaches of probation conditions, including positive drug tests and arrests, the offender remained free until the fatal incident. Michael's parents, Garry and Lesley Hoolickin, have since campaigned for reforms in the Probation Service and co-founded the campaign group VOICE (Victims Oversight In Criminal Enforcement).

During a recent parliamentary session, Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell highlighted the Hoolickin family's plight, stating that Michael's murder was a result of the inadequate monitoring of violent offenders by the Probation Service. The family is advocating for a formal apology from the government to families affected by similar tragedies and is calling for a comprehensive review of the probation system, which statistics indicate has led to one victim every three days.

The Prime Minister's acknowledgment of the Hoolickin case and the broader issues within the probation system may lead to significant discussions about reform. The family hopes that increased scrutiny will prevent future tragedies and ensure that offenders are held accountable for their actions.

articles.title: Medieval Knights to Compete in Full-Contact Combat at The Ashcroft in Whitworth
articles.excerpt: The Ashcroft in Whitworth will host Saturday Knight Fights 6 on September 26, featuring full-contact Medieval combat in an MMA-style cage.
articles.content_html:
Medieval knights will return to Whitworth this month for Saturday Knight Fights 6, an event showcasing full-contact Medieval combat. The competition will take place at The Ashcroft on Saturday, September 26, and is presented by Honour and Arms HMB Ltd, a local club dedicated to the study and competition of historical fighting.

The event promises an evening of excitement as knights clad in full armour engage in battles within an MMA-style cage. Daniel and Mary George, who own and operate Honour and Arms, emphasised the thrilling nature of the fights, stating, "We keep the action rocking and rolling with Saturday Knight Fights 6. Join us for an evening filled with excitement and adrenaline as fighters go head to head in the cage."

Honour and Arms offers workshops and courses on various styles of historical fencing and European martial arts, catering to both beginners and experienced practitioners. The club aims to promote the sport and provide opportunities for enthusiasts to engage in full-contact Medieval combat.

Local residents and visitors are encouraged to attend the event, which is likely to attract a diverse audience interested in historical combat sports. Further details about the event can be found on the Honour and Arms website.

articles.title: Rochdale Residents Urged to Check Voter Registration Ahead of 2027 Elections
articles.excerpt: With local elections scheduled for May 2027, Rochdale Borough Council is reminding residents to verify their voter registration details to ensure they can participate in the upcoming elections.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council is urging residents to check their electoral registration details to avoid losing their chance to vote in the upcoming local elections in May 2027. The council's annual canvass aims to keep the electoral register up to date and identify individuals who may risk losing their voting rights if they are not registered.

Edward McCreadie, elections manager at Rochdale Borough Council, stated that over the summer, emails were sent to residents in more than 40,000 properties, asking them to verify their registration details. Follow-up letters were dispatched this week, and residents are encouraged to keep an eye out for these communications. McCreadie emphasised the importance of ensuring that the information on the electoral register is accurate and up to date, saying, "To make sure you don’t lose your say at upcoming elections, simply follow the instructions sent to you."

Residents who have recently moved homes are particularly urged to check their registration status. Research from the Electoral Commission indicates that recent movers are less likely to be registered compared to those who have lived at the same address for a longer period. In Great Britain, 92% of individuals who have lived in their home for 16 years are registered, while only 36% of those who have lived at an address for less than a year are registered.

Residents aged 16 and above can be added to the electoral register, although they cannot vote until they reach the age of 18. Those wishing to register can do so easily online at rochdale.gov.uk/RegisterToVote. It is crucial for residents to take action now to ensure their participation in the democratic process.

articles.title: Rochdale Sees Rise in Teenagers Seeking Treatment for Addiction
articles.excerpt: More than 170 teenagers in Rochdale received treatment for alcohol and drug abuse, highlighting a growing demand for addiction services in the borough.
articles.content_html:
More than 170 teenagers in Rochdale received treatment for alcohol and drug abuse in the past year, reflecting a significant rise in demand for addiction services among young people and adults. This increase comes as the borough's Health, Schools and Care Overview and Scrutiny Committee prepares to meet on Wednesday to discuss strategies for addressing addiction issues, including tobacco, vaping, drugs, alcohol, and gambling.

In a report to the committee, Kuiama Thompson, Director of Public Health and Communities, stated that drug and alcohol harm continues to significantly impact the health of Rochdale residents. This includes avoidable hospital admissions and premature mortality, which place additional pressure on health and care services and exacerbate health inequalities. The report also noted the broader societal impacts of addiction, such as increased safeguarding concerns, crime, homelessness, and unemployment.

According to figures from the National Drug Treatment Monitoring System, there are approximately 1,831 individuals in Rochdale who use opiates and crack cocaine, alongside 2,905 individuals with alcohol dependency. While there is no evidence of an overall increase in alcohol consumption in the borough, the harm caused by long-term heavy drinking is on the rise, likely due to historical drinking patterns and socio-economic deprivation.

The main substances leading young people to seek treatment include cannabis and alcohol. Ms Thompson highlighted that strong pathways have been established to identify young people presenting with health issues who may not disclose their drug use, ensuring they receive the necessary support.

articles.title: New Café Run by Veterans Opens at Denehurst House in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: A new café managed by veterans has opened in the restored Denehurst House in Rochdale, providing a community space and support for former armed forces personnel.
articles.content_html:
A new café has officially opened in Denehurst House, a 19th-century manor house in Denehurst Park, Rochdale, which has undergone extensive restoration. The café, managed by the Community Interest Company Get Together After Serving (GTAS), will be staffed by veterans and their families, offering a range of hot and cold sandwiches, cakes, breakfasts, tea, and coffee.

The opening ceremony took place on Saturday, September 5, 2026. GTAS was founded by local residents Adam Trennery, Wayne Traynor, and Wayne Simms, aiming to support veterans through various wellbeing programmes and community events. Trennery expressed excitement about the café, highlighting its potential to serve as a base for further veteran support while welcoming the wider community.

Denehurst House, originally built for Alderman Robert Turner in the 1890s, has been restored to retain its period features, including ornate coving and bay windows. The building was previously used as council offices before falling into disrepair. The restoration was commissioned by Rochdale Borough Council, which is also considering using the remaining space in the house for accommodation for local veterans, following a public consultation.

The café will operate daily from 9am to 6pm between May and October and from 9am to 4pm between November and April. The initiative not only revitalises a historic building but also aims to foster community engagement and support for those who have served in the armed forces.

articles.title: Five Lamborghinis and a Mercedes G-Wagon Seized Following Dangerous Driving Reports on M66 and M62
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police seized six high-performance vehicles in Rochdale as part of a crackdown on anti-social driving, following reports of dangerous behaviour on the M66.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

13:11, 03 September 2026

Greater Manchester Police seized six high-performance vehicles in Rochdale as part of a crackdown on anti-social driving, following reports of dangerous behaviour on the M66.

Officers from Greater Manchester Police’s Transport Policing and Crime Command (TPACC) seized six luxury cars in Rochdale last night as part of a crackdown on anti-social and dangerous driving. The operation followed reports of reckless driving involving high-powered vehicles, including Lamborghinis and Mercedes G-Wagons, on the M66.

Witnesses reported that the vehicles were being driven at excessive speeds, weaving across lanes, and performing wheel spins, with some slowing down to speeds as low as 17mph on the motorway. Police located the convoy on the M62 and successfully stopped two Lamborghinis as they exited the motorway. The remaining vehicles were brought to a halt using specialist tactics in Rochdale.

Five Lamborghinis and one Mercedes G-Wagon were seized under Section 59 of the Police Reform Act 2002. In addition to the vehicle seizures, the drivers of the offending vehicles are facing prosecution for multiple driving offences.

Chief Inspector Danny Kabal of GMP’s TPACC stated, “We take road safety very seriously in GMP, and we will not tolerate careless, inconsiderate, anti-social or dangerous driving on our roads.” This operation highlights the police's commitment to ensuring safety on local roads and addressing the concerns of residents regarding reckless driving.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Rejects Late-Night Car Wash Proposal on Kingsway
articles.excerpt: A proposed late-night car wash on Kingsway has been refused by Rochdale Council following concerns from local residents about noise and traffic impact.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has unanimously rejected a proposal for a late-night car wash on Kingsway, following significant concerns from local residents regarding noise and traffic impact. The application, submitted by Moonbeam Car Wash, sought to establish five self-service jet wash bays, alongside a laundrette pod, a dog wash pod, and a vending machine, on the site of the former Paul Price Cars dealership.

During a planning committee meeting on September 2, residents expressed their worries about the potential disruption caused by the car wash's operating hours, which were proposed to be from 8am to 11pm. A representative from the Merinall Close residents highlighted that the area already suffers from parking issues, stating, "Residents already experience vehicles parking outside the site. We have evidence of real world conditions being in this area."

Councillor Shakil Ahmed questioned how the developer could justify the operation of the car wash without supervision, while Matthew Gray, representing Moonbeam, claimed that a noise impact assessment had been accepted by Environmental Health. He noted that the original proposal for a 24-hour operation had been reduced to the current hours in response to community concerns, and that measures such as fencing and planting would be implemented to mitigate noise.

Despite these assurances, Councillor Sameena Zaheer raised concerns about the additional traffic on Kingsway, stating, "Most of the time Kingsway is a packed road. It is going to add more to this." The planning committee ultimately decided to refuse the application, citing noise, traffic impact, and the effect on residential amenity as key factors in their decision.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says ‘cruckle’
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the little local verb 'cruckle': what it means, where it comes from, and why Rochdalians still cling to it.
articles.summary: A short guide to the little local verb 'cruckle': what it means, where it comes from, and why Rochdalians still cling to it.
articles.body:
Anyone who grew up in parts of Rochdale will recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” In everyday local speech cruckle is used to mean going over on, or twisting, the ankle — that awkward stumble you can usually walk off but that still makes you wince. This modern, conversational sense is widely reported in contemporary accounts of Rochdale speech. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

But cruckle is not a recent invention. Late nineteenth‑century dialect lexicography records an older verb crookle (also seen spelled crookle/crockle/cruckle in some sources) meaning “to bend, make crooked, stoop or hobble.” That semantic field — bending, limping, or hobbling — easily covers both the older senses and the narrow modern one about rolling an ankle. The English Dialect Dictionary compiled by Joseph Wright is the principal historical source for this family of forms. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

How did crookle become locally recognisable as cruckle in Rochdale? Dialect historians point to ordinary sound‑change and word‑formation processes: the base crook (a bend or hook) plus a frequentative/diminutive suffix ‑le (a familiar pattern in northern and Midland English) produces a verb meaning ‘to bend repeatedly or slightly’ — crook → crookle → cruckle in pronunciation. Comparative work on Germanic dialects shows related forms (kreukelen, krökeln, etc.), which helps explain the family’s meaning and shape. In short, cruckle is best seen as a local survival and reflex of an older dialect verb‑group, preserved in local speech. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

Is cruckle unique to Rochdale? Popular feeling in the borough treats it as a Rochdale speciality, and perceptual‑dialect research supports that association: in a recent draw‑a‑map study of Greater Manchester, respondents repeatedly used words and keywords tied to Rochdale — the authors include cruckle among locally salient labels that people use when describing the town’s speech. That is, people in the region identify cruckle as a Rochdale‑flavour word, even if closely related forms were recorded historically across parts of Lancashire and neighbouring counties. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

What does dialect research tell us beyond etymology and perception? Two points matter. First, folk‑linguistic studies show that local pride and visibility keep words alive: when people point to a term as “our word,” its social value rises and its use is reinforced across generations. Second, dialect atlases and historical dictionaries reveal that many words that now feel highly local had wider past distributions; what looks exclusive today can be the last local stronghold of a once broader regional term. In other words, cruckle’s apparent Rochdale exclusivity is as much about social identity and perception as it is about unique etymology. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

So what should Rochdalians take from this? Cruckle is a neat example of how small vocabulary items carry history and identity: its roots run into nineteenth‑century dialect lexicons and further back into Germanic patterns, while its present‑day life is shaped by local use and local recognition. It is not, strictly speaking, an invention only ever used inside the borough — historical records show kin‑forms elsewhere — but today it survives, thrives and signals “Rochdale” in the way only a handful of truly local words do. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

articles.title: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing Appoints New Chair
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing reports significant progress in rehousing residents from the Seven Sisters tower blocks, with over 600 homes now vacant following safety concerns.
articles.content_html:
More than 600 homes are currently empty in Rochdale following the decision by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) to evict the remaining residents from the Seven Sisters tower blocks, officially known as College Bank. This decision was announced in October 2025 and has led to a significant reduction in the number of households living in the area, with only around 100 households still awaiting relocation out of approximately 760 total flats.

The eviction process, which was initially met with shock by residents, was clarified by RBH to take place over an 18-month period. As of late August 2026, 117 households have accepted offers for new accommodation, with 82 having already moved and a further 35 in the process of relocating. The remaining residents are primarily those who have not yet found suitable housing, as many have left due to what RBH describes as 'natural attrition', which includes reasons such as tenancy endings or voluntary departures.

The need for these evictions arose from safety concerns identified in a recent building survey. The survey highlighted various issues, including structural and electrical problems, water pumping system failures, roof damage, and rising costs for heating and lighting. RBH has stated that all tenants will receive support during their transition to new homes, including financial assistance for those affected. Leaseholders will have their properties purchased at market value.

This situation has been ongoing for nearly a decade, with plans for the demolition of some of the high-rises initially proposed in 2017. Although demolition was ruled out in 2023, RBH has since reopened discussions about the future of the tower blocks, stating that no final decision has been made regarding potential demolition. Local campaigners from the Save the Seven Sisters group have expressed concerns about the implications of these developments, fearing that the evictions may lead to a permanent loss of housing in the area.

articles.title: Rochdale Secures First EFL Win with 3-0 Victory Over Shrewsbury
articles.excerpt: Rochdale achieved their first win since returning to the EFL, defeating Shrewsbury 3-0 at the Crown Oil Arena, with manager Ian Watson praising the team's performance.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Football Club celebrated their first victory since returning to the English Football League (EFL) with a commanding 3-0 win against Shrewsbury Town at the Crown Oil Arena on 1 September 2026. The match marked a significant milestone for manager Ian Watson, who expressed his satisfaction with the team's performance.

Baba Adeeko opened the scoring for Rochdale in the 33rd minute, converting a rebound after a blocked shot from Emmanuel Dieseruvwe. Just before half-time, Luke Hannant doubled the lead with a well-placed finish over Shrewsbury goalkeeper Will Brook, capitalising on a defensive error. The home side maintained their dominance throughout the match, with goalkeeper Nils Ramming making a crucial save to deny Will Boyle's header early in the second half.

Substitute Jonny Smith sealed the victory in the 80th minute, scoring with a curling shot into the roof of the net. This win not only provided the team with three points but also showcased the courage and bravery that Watson had been seeking from his players.

Following the match, Watson highlighted the importance of the performance over the scoreline, stating, "We needed to get that first win over the line. The boys want to win so much and run so hard that it can sometimes manifest as anxiety. Tonight, we played without fear, and that is how we need to continue moving forward."

articles.title: Tram Services Disruption in Rochdale This Weekend
articles.excerpt: No trams will operate between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre until 2pm on Saturday, with further service changes expected on Sunday due to maintenance works.
articles.content_html:
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has announced that there will be no tram services operating between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre this Saturday until 2pm. This disruption is part of ongoing maintenance and improvement works on the network.

Additionally, on Sunday, tram services will be affected from the start of service until 11am due to works at Deansgate-Castlefield and Trafford Bar. Passengers are advised to plan their journeys accordingly, as these changes may lead to delays and altered service patterns across the network.

TfGM is also addressing accessibility issues at several tram stops. The lift at Derker tram stop is currently out of service, and passengers travelling towards Manchester can use a ramp from Cromford Street to access the platform. For those heading away from Manchester, a ramp and track crossing are available for access to the Rochdale bound platform.

At Failsworth tram stop, both lifts are out of service while replacement works are carried out. Passengers requiring step-free access are advised to travel to Hollinwood to connect with services. For further assistance, customers can contact the Metrolink customer service centre at 0161 244 1000, available from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends.
